A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and included appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual safety evaluations, attribution and token-perturbation experiments, and Hindi/Bengali human validation, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds social-media evaluation, expanded human validation, translation-based restoration, utility evaluation, and mixing-ratio experiments.

M1.justification: Section 9 adds a defensive preprocessing procedure: detect prompts containing at least 30% non-English tokens, translate the entire prompt into English, and query the model without computing attribution at inference time. This differs substantively from v1's experiments translating selected English tokens into other languages. The underlying SDA procedure remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 Section 5.3 extends evaluation beyond synthetic prompts to authentic Hindi-English Facebook comments from TRAC-1. This adds a materially different input domain and natural code-mixing scenario. The original ten-language Generic and Local TestSets remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated model set remains phi-4B, mistral-7B, and llama-3.1-8B. No competing defense or attribution method is newly evaluated. The translation layer is a new proposed intervention, while its English and untreated code-mixed controls already appear in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a three-condition restoration evaluation on llama-3.1-8B, answerability/topicality utility judging, and four additional Bengali-English mixing ratios. Human validation expands from harmful/non-harmful/ambiguous response labeling to binary harmfulness judgments for English and code-mixed responses plus translation-quality assessment. These are new or revised evaluation designs; the original Table 1 comparison remains.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds mixing-ratio sensitivity analysis, and Appendix B tests whether restoration sacrifices answerability or topicality. Human validation also broadens to six languages and checks translation quality. The original toxic versus less-toxic token perturbations and three qualitative behavioral cases are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports language-specific Cohen's kappa, model-disagreement rates, and ambiguity rates in Table 5. v2 replaces this reporting with task-specific Fleiss' kappa in Section 6 and removes the explicit disagreement/ambiguity rates. Appendix E newly discloses fixed-seed deterministic inference; it does not establish additional repeated runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical results are unchanged. New results include TRAC-1 ASRs of 61.32%, 74.87%, and 79.24% for phi, Mistral, and LLaMA respectively; restoration reducing LLaMA's Local TestSet macro ASR from 84.08% to 76.98%; utility scores of 0.87 versus 0.86; and mixing-ratio results in Table 7. Six-language human results and numerical attribution plots also add evidence beyond v1. These are added evaluations, not improvements to the original same-setting results.

T1.justification: Appendix B introduces a mathematical definition of utility as the fraction of outputs judged both answerable and topical. The existing rank-inverse, saliency-drift, and targeted-perturbation definitions remain equivalent, and no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: v2's abstract and introduction add claims of generalization to real-world social-media inputs and a translation-based defense recovering roughly 80% of safety lost to code-mixing. These extend v1's principal vulnerability, attribution, and cultural-sensitivity contributions. SDA itself was already introduced in v1; its prominence in the rewritten abstract is not a new contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets natural-data and mixing-ratio results as evidence that failures are distributional and that the fixed 60:40 setting may underestimate web risks. Section 9 presents English-pivot restoration as causal support for the attribution explanation, while explicitly limiting it to a probe rather than a complete deployment solution. Appendix B adds an interpretation concerning preservation of utility.

D1.justification: New Appendix E supplies previously absent hardware specifications, operating-system and library versions, inference software, attribution tooling, and zero-temperature decoding information. Section 6 documents Prolific recruitment, three native annotators per example, majority voting, and anonymization/shuffling. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation, although the translation model and evaluation sample counts remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 adds Kumar et al. (2018), Benchmarking Aggression Identification in Social Media, to support the TRAC-1 evaluation. The existing related-work discussion and other cited works are retained; citation renumbering and bibliographic formatting changes do not constitute additional research-positioning changes.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, the introduction and experimental rationale receive targeted additions, and human validation becomes a main-text section. Appendices are reorganized around the added material, and affiliations and citation style change. Most existing explanatory prose, attribution discussion, key insights, and conclusion are retained, so this is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 changes document-wide typography, page layout, author presentation, and caption styling. Main-text Figures 4–6 become numerical attribution bar displays; word clouds appear in the appendix, with the Case 1 clouds revised and Cases 2–3 retained. Human-validation tables are redesigned, and restoration and mixing-ratio tables are added. These extend well beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful evidence beyond v1's synthetic evaluations and limited human checks, particularly restoration with a utility control, mixing-ratio sensitivity, and broader validation. Execution details also improve reproducibility. The net gain is limited by unspecified evaluation sample counts and translation machinery, removal of explicit GPT-4o disagreement rates, and claims exceeding the reported evidence: inter-annotator kappa does not explicitly establish GPT-4o agreement, and Table 3 claims reductions across all ten languages despite an unchanged Russian ASR.
